title: Thyroid surgery: nerves and parathyroids at risk

variants.label: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve injury

claims: The recurrent laryngeal nerves are branches of the vagus: the left hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum, the right hooks under the right subclavian artery.
Both recurrent laryngeal nerves ascend in the tracheo-oesophageal groove and enter the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint.
The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid.

The inferior thyroid artery (from the thyrocervical trunk) crosses the recurrent laryngeal nerve near the lower pole of the thyroid; this crossing and the nerve's entry into the larynx (near the ligament of Berry) are where it is most often injured in thyroidectomy.
Unilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury causes hoarseness (paralysed vocal fold); bilateral injury causes stridor and airway obstruction.
The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery (first branch of the external carotid) toward the upper pole and supplies cricothyroid.
Cricothyroid tenses the vocal folds; external branch of superior laryngeal nerve injury causes loss of high-pitched voice and voice fatigue.
The internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve is sensory to the larynx above the vocal folds; its loss impairs the cough reflex.
The parathyroid glands lie on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes and are supplied mainly by the inferior thyroid artery.
Removal or devascularisation of the parathyroids in thyroidectomy causes hypocalcaemia with low PTH: perioral tingling, cramps, Chvostek and Trousseau signs.
Chvostek sign: tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear causes facial twitching. Trousseau sign: an inflated blood pressure cuff causes carpal spasm.
Severe post-thyroidectomy hypocalcaemia is treated with IV calcium gluconate.
